strengths: The paper identifies a concrete and important failure mode for activation quantization of large ViT-style vision encoders: middle-layer activation outliers/sink tokens that dominate the quantization range. The empirical analysis linking layerwise quantization sensitivity to maximum token norms is convincing and well motivated.

RegCache is a simple, training-free plug-in idea: curate universal middle-layer register candidates, insert their averaged KV caches as prefixes, and delete emerging high-norm tokens. The adaptation from LLM attention-sink prefixing to vision encoders is original enough and technically plausible.

The experimental coverage is broad: CLIP, OpenCLIP, SigLIP, SigLIP2, and DINOv2; multiple PTQ baselines; ImageNet classification; MS-COCO retrieval; additional transfer datasets; FIMA-Q, AWQ, and Hadamard-rotation combinations in the appendix. This gives a reasonably strong case that the method is not tied to a single backbone or quantizer.

Ablations support the proposed design: caching and deletion are shown to be complementary, RegCache substantially reduces maximum token norms, and the comparison to test-time registers suggests the method is better targeted to quantization.

The method has practical appeal because it requires no model retraining and appears to add little FLOP overhead, while producing large gains in several difficult W6A6/W8A8 settings where naive activation quantization collapses.
weaknesses: The method is less calibration-free than the presentation sometimes implies. It uses 50k ImageNet training images, reference-task accuracy to find sensitive layers, and per-model/per-quantizer tuning of prefix copy count and deletion count. This is a meaningful extra validation procedure, may require labels, and is not fully comparable to PTQ baselines calibrated with far fewer samples.

The strongest improvements are often in regimes where the baseline is catastrophically broken, while gains over stronger PTQ methods at W8A8 are frequently modest. At W4A4 many results remain unusably low despite improvement, so the practical low-bit impact is mixed.

The evaluation focuses on global classification and retrieval. Since the method deletes image tokens and modifies attention with cached prefixes, its effect on dense/localization tasks, segmentation, detection, VLM perception pipelines, or patch-level representations is not established, despite the motivation around general vision encoders.

Deployment claims need more care. The paper discusses static activation quantization and edge hardware motivation, but the experiments appear to rely largely on pseudo/dynamic per-tensor quantization and report limited wall-clock measurements. There is no demonstration with actual int8 kernels, memory traffic analysis, or hardware targets representative of the stated applications.

Important reproducibility details are underspecified or scattered: exact selected layers, numbers of copied prefixes, numbers of deleted tokens, sensitivity-search protocol, calibration/reference data requirements, and whether labels are used for tuning should be tabulated for every backbone and baseline.

The theoretical component is weak: the cosine-similarity lemma mainly formalizes the obvious fact that vectors with a shared large coordinate become similar. It explains an observation but does not substantially justify why such aligned outlier coordinates arise or why cached averaged KV prefixes should reliably work.

The method can slightly hurt some strong baselines/settings, e.g. DINOv2 W8A8 with PTQ baselines and SigLIP2 with FIMA-Q, suggesting the hyperparameter search and token deletion can be brittle. The paper would benefit from failure-case analysis and confidence intervals over calibration subsets.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practical problem: activation quantization of large vision encoders, where outlier activations can strongly degrade PTQ performance even at W8A8.

The central empirical observation, that outlier-prone/sink-like tokens in vision encoders tend to emerge in middle layers and can be similar across images, is interesting and potentially useful for understanding ViT quantization behavior.

RegCache is simple in spirit and compatible with several existing PTQ methods. The experiments cover multiple vision encoders, quantization methods, bitwidths, and tasks, and the reported gains are sometimes large, especially for W6A6/W8A8 settings where naive activation quantization collapses.

The paper includes useful ablations and analyses, including norm reduction, prefix/deletion ablations, cross-dataset transfer of prefixes, FIMA-Q results, weight-only quantization, latency/FLOP estimates, and comparison to a test-time register baseline.
weaknesses: The method is less convincingly 'training-free' or generally deployable than claimed. It requires identifying sensitive layers, selecting register candidates from 50k ImageNet training images, and tuning the number of prefix and deleted tokens on a reference task. This is a substantial task- and model-dependent calibration/search procedure, and the paper does not sufficiently separate this cost from standard PTQ calibration budgets.

The evaluation risks being overly tuned to ImageNet. The same ImageNet training distribution is used to select sensitive layers, build/register prefixes, and tune hyperparameters, while ImageNet validation is the main headline benchmark. The cross-dataset results are helpful but mostly compare against naive quantization, not the full set of strong PTQ baselines with and without RegCache, so they do not fully resolve the concern.

Several results suggest the method is brittle. At W4A4 many entries remain essentially unusable, DINOv2 sometimes drops relative to baselines, SigLIP2 with FIMA-Q slightly worsens in classification, and the ablation shows that prefix caching or token deletion alone can severely hurt. This raises concerns about robustness and about how reliably practitioners can tune the method outside the reported settings.

The deployment story is underdeveloped. The paper discusses FLOPs and wall-clock time, but the measurements appear to use pseudo-quantization rather than real integer kernels on target hardware. Since the motivation is compute/energy reduction on edge devices, the lack of end-to-end int8 deployment evidence weakens the practical impact claim.

The comparison to prior register/sink-token methods is somewhat narrow. RegCache is clearly inspired by attention-sink prefixing and test-time registers, but the paper does not provide a deep enough comparison of calibration cost, implementation complexity, and accuracy/latency tradeoffs against the closest alternatives under matched settings.

The theoretical component is very limited: the cosine-similarity lemma mainly formalizes the obvious fact that large aligned coordinates dominate cosine similarity. It does not substantially explain why such aligned outlier channels arise or when RegCache should work or fail.

Reproducibility details are incomplete for a method with many hidden choices: exact sensitive-layer selection protocol, validation splits, calibration/reference-task usage per baseline, token deletion counts, prefix counts, and how these are selected for each model/quantizer are not reported in enough detail to independently reproduce the tables.

Overall, the paper has interesting observations and some strong empirical gains, but the claims are weakened by tuning/calibration ambiguity, incomplete deployment validation, and signs of brittleness. I would lean slightly against acceptance unless these issues are clarified and the evaluation is tightened under fair, fixed calibration budgets.

strengths: The paper identifies a clear and practically important problem: activation outliers make W/A quantization of large ViT-based vision encoders fragile, even at 8-bit in some settings. The connection between layerwise quantization sensitivity and high-norm middle-layer tokens is well motivated and useful for the community.

RegCache is a simple, training-free plug-in idea with a plausible mechanism: find universal middle-layer register-like tokens, cache their KV representations, prefix them before sensitive layers, and delete internally emerging sink tokens. The distinction from LLM attention-sink prefixing is convincing: vision encoders lack fixed semantic sink tokens and outliers emerge after early image processing.

The experimental coverage is strong for an algorithms/general submission. Results span CLIP, OpenCLIP, SigLIP, SigLIP2, and DINOv2, multiple PTQ baselines, 4/6/8-bit settings, ImageNet classification, COCO retrieval, and several transfer classification datasets. The improvements are often substantial, especially in W6A6 and difficult W8A8 cases such as CLIP/OpenCLIP/SigLIP2 naive quantization.

The paper includes helpful analysis and ablations: foreground/background experiments, cosine similarity of outlier tokens, norm reduction after RegCache, component ablations for caching/deletion, transfer of ImageNet-searched prefixes to other datasets, overhead estimates, and appendix experiments with FIMA-Q, AWQ, and Hadamard-rotation quantization.

The method has favorable practical properties: no model retraining, small reported FLOP overhead, and compatibility with existing quantization methods. The limitations section honestly notes the need for heuristic hyperparameter choices.
weaknesses: The method is not quite as calibration-free as the presentation sometimes suggests. It uses 50k ImageNet training images, layer sensitivity sweeps, validation/reference-task accuracy, and searches over prefix copies and deleted-token counts. This is acceptable for PTQ, but the paper should be clearer about calibration cost, label dependence, and how performance changes with much smaller or unlabeled calibration sets.

The gains are uneven. W4A4 remains largely unusable for many models despite RegCache, DINOv2 shows negligible or negative gains in some settings, and strong baselines such as FIMA-Q or SigLIP/SigLIP2 cases sometimes improve only marginally or even drop slightly. The claims of consistent improvement should be softened to reflect these cases.

The deployment story is incomplete. Experiments appear to rely on pseudo/dynamic per-tensor quantization and reported latency over whole validation runs rather than a demonstrated optimized int8 kernel path on edge hardware. Since the motivation emphasizes real-time edge inference and compute-bound settings, stronger hardware evidence would make the practical impact more convincing.

The token deletion step may be problematic for tasks needing dense spatial correspondence or patch-level outputs, yet the evaluation focuses on global classification/retrieval. Because the method removes image tokens at inference, tests on detection, segmentation, dense retrieval, or VLM downstream tasks would be important for judging broader applicability.

Some methodological details are underspecified for reproducibility: exact selected layers, searched hyperparameters per model/baseline, calibration/evaluation splits used for tuning, and whether the tuning procedure risks overfitting to ImageNet-style classification. A compact table of final RegCache configurations would help.

Originality is solid but incremental rather than transformative. The core idea adapts recent attention-sink/prefixing concepts from LLM quantization and register-token observations in ViTs; the main novelty is the middle-layer vision-specific formulation and empirical validation rather than a fundamentally new quantization theory.

strengths: The paper identifies a concrete and important failure mode for activation quantization of large vision encoders: middle-layer activation outliers/sink tokens that strongly expand per-tensor quantization ranges. The empirical analysis connecting layerwise quantization sensitivity with high-norm FC2 inputs is useful and relevant.

RegCache is a simple, training-free and modular idea: curate universal register-like outlier tokens, inject their KV caches around sensitive layers, and delete remaining high-norm internal sink tokens. The method is well motivated by the observed differences between LLM and vision-encoder outliers.

The experimental scope is strong: CLIP, OpenCLIP, SigLIP, SigLIP2, DINOv2, multiple PTQ baselines, zero-shot classification, retrieval, VLM image/video tasks, additional datasets, latency measurements, and ablations. The gains are often large, especially in 6-bit and some 4-bit settings, and the method generally improves strong baselines rather than only naive quantization.

The paper includes useful analyses beyond benchmark tables, including outlier norm reduction, prefix insertion layer sensitivity, comparison with test-time registers, a label-free reconstruction-loss variant, segmentation considerations, weight-only quantization, Hadamard rotation, and SmoothQuant combinations.
The latency study suggests that the proposed cache/deletion mechanism adds little overhead in INT8 deployment, supporting the practical motivation for efficient vision encoders.
weaknesses: The method is described as training-free, but it still requires a fairly involved model- and quantizer-specific search: identifying sensitive layers, curating from 50k ImageNet training images, tuning the number of prefix copies, and tuning deleted-token counts on a reference task. This weakens the practical simplicity claim and raises reproducibility concerns unless all selected layers and hyperparameters are fully released.

The strongest gains are concentrated in settings where the baseline collapses, while several strong-baseline W8A8 results improve only marginally and DINOv2 sometimes degrades. The paper would benefit from a clearer discussion of when RegCache is expected to help versus when modern PTQ already handles the outliers.

The 4-bit results remain very poor in many cases despite improvements, e.g. several W4A4 classification/retrieval numbers are still near zero. The claim of strong value in extremely low-bit regimes should be qualified: RegCache can rescue some models/settings but does not make 4-bit activation quantization broadly reliable.

The token deletion step may be problematic for spatially structured downstream tasks because it removes patch tokens. The segmentation experiment is helpful but narrow: only W8A8 SigLIP-B/16 is shown, and the interpolation workaround is not integrated into the main method or evaluated broadly.

The implementation details of KV-cache insertion in non-autoregressive ViTs, interaction with static activation quantization, and deployment constraints are not fully clear from the main text. In particular, the reported latency is for INT8, while much of the accuracy motivation is around W4A4/W6A6, where hardware support and realized speedups may differ substantially.

The universality claim is plausible but only partially established. The register candidates are selected from ImageNet, and cross-dataset classification helps, but broader domain-shift tests, robustness to calibration-set size/composition, and results on detection/segmentation/VLM architectures beyond a few cases would make the claim more convincing.

Some ablation results are surprising, such as prefix-only or delete-only sometimes being worse than the baseline, but the paper does not fully explain these failure modes. A deeper analysis would help users understand how brittle the method is to hyperparameter choices.

strengths: The paper tackles a relevant practical problem: activation quantization of large pretrained vision encoders, especially for VLM and video settings where encoder cost is meaningful.

The central observation, that outlier/sink behavior in vision encoders emerges in middle layers and differs from LLM attention sinks, is interesting and reasonably motivated by layerwise sensitivity, foreground/background analysis, and cross-image cosine similarity.

RegCache is simple, training-free in the sense of not updating model weights, and designed as a plug-in on top of existing PTQ methods. This makes the method practically attractive if the search and implementation details are reproducible.
The empirical coverage is broad: CLIP, OpenCLIP, SigLIP, SigLIP2, DINOv2, Qwen3-VL, LLaVA, classification, retrieval, VQA, and video benchmarks are considered, with multiple PTQ baselines.
The method gives large gains in several difficult settings, especially W6A6/W8A8 and some W4A4 cases, and latency measurements suggest the additional inference overhead is small.

Ablations and supplementary experiments address several natural questions, including prefix caching versus deletion, reconstruction-loss-based selection, weight-only quantization, Hadamard rotation, and comparison to test-time register mechanisms.
weaknesses: The novelty is somewhat incremental relative to attention-sink prefixing for LLM quantization and recent work on registers/test-time registers in ViTs. The paper’s main contribution is an adaptation and search procedure for vision encoders rather than a fundamentally new quantization principle.

The method is not as cleanly “training-free” or deployment-simple as advertised: it relies on identifying sensitive layers, curating tokens from 50k ImageNet training images, and tuning the number of prefix/deleted tokens using reference-task accuracy. This supervised, model- and baseline-specific search weakens the plug-and-play claim.

There is a potential evaluation concern around using ImageNet training data and ImageNet classification accuracy to tune hyperparameters, then reporting ImageNet validation accuracy as a main result. The cross-dataset table helps, but the paper should more clearly separate selection data, calibration data, and evaluation data.

The gains are uneven. DINOv2 sees negligible or negative improvements in several settings, and many W4A4 results remain essentially unusable despite RegCache. The paper’s language sometimes overstates consistency relative to these mixed cases.

Token deletion is a potentially risky operation because it changes the token set and may remove spatial information. Dense prediction is only lightly evaluated with one ADE20K/SigLIP W8A8 setting and an interpolation workaround, so the safety of deletion for spatial tasks is not convincingly established.

The theoretical component is weak: the cosine-similarity lemma mostly states that shared large coordinates dominate cosine similarity. It does not substantially explain why such aligned outliers arise or why the cached register should generalize across architectures and tasks.

The ablation table reveals that prefix-only or deletion-only can severely hurt performance for some models, implying the method is brittle and dependent on careful tuning. This deserves a deeper failure-mode analysis.

Reproducibility details are incomplete for a method with many choices: exact searched layers, selected token counts, deletion counts, validation protocols, calibration/reference splits, quantizer implementation details, and per-baseline hyperparameters should be specified more explicitly.
The paper does not report statistical variability, confidence intervals, or repeated runs for token curation/search, making it hard to judge robustness of the reported gains.

The comparison to concurrent test-time register work is limited to two models under W8A8 ImageNet. Given the conceptual proximity, a broader and more carefully controlled comparison would strengthen the originality case.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and original contribution for Algorithms/General: RegCache is a training-free plug-in mechanism for activation-outlier mitigation in quantized vision encoders, based on the interesting observation that middle-layer outlier tokens become highly similar across images and can be replaced by cached register-like prefixes.

The motivation is technically compelling. The paper carefully distinguishes vision encoders from LLMs, especially the delayed emergence of sink/outlier tokens due to continuous visual tokenization, and supports this with layerwise sensitivity, foreground/background, cosine-similarity, and registered-DINO analyses.

The experimental evidence is broad and generally strong. Results cover CLIP, OpenCLIP, SigLIP, SigLIP2, and DINOv2; multiple PTQ baselines including PTQ4ViT, RepQ-ViT, NoisyQuant, FIMA-Q, and ERQ; image classification, image-text retrieval, VLM image/video benchmarks, and additional transfer datasets.

The gains are especially meaningful in the low-bit regimes where activation outliers are most damaging. In several W4A4 and W6A6 settings RegCache substantially improves otherwise collapsed quantized models, and it also improves Qwen3-VL and LLaVA-family VLM results under 4-bit vision-encoder quantization.

The method is practical in spirit: it requires no retraining, can be layered on top of existing quantization pipelines, and the latency measurements with TensorRT show only around 1-1.5% overhead for standalone encoders and negligible overhead in the tested VLM setting.

The paper includes useful ablations and analyses, including norm reduction, prefix caching versus token deletion, generalization of ImageNet-searched prefixes to other datasets, reconstruction-loss-based selection, weight-only quantization, Hadamard rotation combinations, and comparison to a concurrent test-time register idea.
weaknesses: The method depends on several heuristically selected hyperparameters, including the sensitive layer, number of prefix copies, insertion layer, and number of deleted tokens. The paper acknowledges this, but the tuning burden may be nontrivial when moving to new encoders, quantizers, or deployment domains.

The main selection procedure uses ImageNet-1k training data and reference-task accuracy, which weakens the claim of broad plug-and-play deployment. The label-free reconstruction-loss alternative is encouraging, but it is only shown on a subset of models/settings and sometimes gives smaller or mixed gains.

Some results are less uniformly strong than the headline suggests. DINOv2 sees negligible or negative average gains in W8A8 with several baselines, token deletion alone can be highly destructive, and even with RegCache some extreme W4A4 settings remain near unusable depending on the model and quantizer.

The interaction between deleting patch tokens and tasks requiring spatial fidelity is not fully resolved. The ADE20K experiment with interpolation is helpful, but it is limited to one model/setting, and broader dense prediction or localization evaluations would be needed before concluding the approach is generally safe beyond global representation tasks.

The paper would benefit from more implementation detail for reproducibility: exact searched hyperparameters per model/baseline, candidate-token construction details, calibration/reference splits, and whether any validation choices leak benchmark-specific assumptions should be tabulated more explicitly.

The conceptual explanation for outlier-token universality is plausible but mostly empirical and stylized. The lemma explains why shared high-magnitude channels imply high cosine similarity, but it does not explain why those channels align across diverse images and architectures in the first place.
